content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In Christian teaching and biblical scholarship, 'to know' (Hebrew yada'; Greek ginōskō) is overwhelmingly interpreted as denoting intimate, experiential, relational knowledge rather than mere intellectual or factual awareness. 'Knowing God' is read as personal communion and covenant relationship with Him, and being 'known' by God as His personal, saving recognition and acceptance. Eternal life itself is defined as this relational knowledge (John 17:3).", "primary_basis": ["John 17:3 ('this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God')", "Jeremiah 9:23-24 ('let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me')", "Jeremiah 31:34 ('they shall all know me, from the least to the greatest')", "Hosea 6:6 ('I desire... the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings')", "Hosea 4:1, 4:6 (Israel destroyed for lack of knowledge of God)", "Matthew 7:23 ('I never knew you; depart from me')", "Philippians 3:8-10 ('that I may know him and the power of his resurrection')", "1 John 2:3-4; 4:7-8 (knowing God evidenced by obedience and love)", "Galatians 4:9 ('now that you know God, or rather are known by God')", "Psalm 1:6 ('the LORD knows the way of the righteous')", "Exodus 33:12-17 ('I know you by name')", "John 10:14-15 ('I know my own and my own know me')"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "Sexual/marital euphemism: 'to know' as the idiom for sexual intercourse, widely treated as an extension of the intimacy sense and often used homiletically to illustrate that biblical knowledge is union, not information.", "basis": ["Genesis 4:1 ('Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived')", "Genesis 4:17; 4:25", "Genesis 19:8; Judges 11:39; 19:22-25", "Matthew 1:25 ('knew her not until she had given birth')", "Luke 1:34 ('since I know not a man')"], "prominence": "dominant"}, {"meaning": "Covenantal election: 'to know' as God's sovereign choice or election of persons/Israel ('foreknew' = 'fore-loved/chose'), a standard reading in Reformed and much critical scholarship, drawing on ancient Near Eastern treaty language where 'know' means 'recognize as covenant partner.'", "basis": ["Amos 3:2 ('You only have I known of all the families of the earth')", "Romans 8:29 ('those whom he foreknew he also predestined')", "Genesis 18:19 ('I have known/chosen him')", "Jeremiah 1:5 ('before I formed you in the womb I knew you')", "2 Timothy 2:19 ('the Lord knows those who are his')"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Moral-experiential autonomy: in the phrase 'knowledge of good and evil' (Genesis 2-3), 'knowing' read as seizing autonomous moral determination or experiential acquaintance with evil, rather than gaining information; variously nuanced as moral autonomy, maturity, or comprehensive knowledge (a merism).", "basis": ["Genesis 2:9, 2:17", "Genesis 3:5, 3:22 ('you will be like God, knowing good and evil')", "Deuteronomy 1:39 (children who 'have no knowledge of good or evil')"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Salvific gnosis: knowledge as secret, esoteric insight that itself saves, characteristic of ancient Gnosticism and rejected by mainstream Christianity; New Testament warnings against 'knowledge falsely so called' are read as opposing this view.", "basis": ["1 Timothy 6:20 ('contradictions of what is falsely called knowledge')", "1 Corinthians 8:1 ('knowledge puffs up, but love builds up')", "Colossians 2:8, 2:18 (often read against proto-gnostic tendencies)"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "Purely intellectual/propositional knowledge: 'to know' as cognitive assent to facts or doctrine; generally treated in Christian interpretation as insufficient by itself, with James cited to show even demons possess such knowledge.", "basis": ["James 2:19 ('even the demons believe—and shudder')", "Romans 1:21 ('although they knew God, they did not honor him')", "Titus 1:16 ('they profess to know God, but deny him by their works')"], "prominence": "minority"}], "has_settled_consensus": true, "confidence": "high", "notes": "There is a broad, recognizable consensus across Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant, and academic biblical scholarship that biblical 'knowing' is relational and experiential (Hebrew yada'), embracing intimacy, covenant loyalty, and obedience, in contrast to Greek notions of detached intellectual cognition (a contrast sometimes overstated in older word-study literature, as critics like James Barr noted). The sexual euphemism (Gen 4:1) and the covenantal-election sense (Amos 3:2; Rom 8:29) are standard, widely acknowledged sub-senses of the same relational root rather than competing symbols. Assessment made blind to the author's material, as instructed."}
